I have been playing Warframe for about a year and a half and have some 3k+ hours recorded and I am currently at Master Level 20.
In Summary, the game is pretty and can be fun if you like killing AI however as most players get bored of playing in a relatively short time I would not advise investing any cash in the game before you have played for more than 500 hours or it will be wasted.
Warframes was orginally all player versus bots with the standard set of fps challenges from the likes of unreal tournament, the game used procedurally generated maps based around 4 tiles sets (void, derelict, grineer,corpus). The last 2 tile sets allowed the developer to lay out a series of missions of supposedly increasing difficulty based opon the solar system, each planet having a number of similar maps with the same enemy (grineer or corpus) to dispatch. In addition to the solar system there are two other areas void and derelict, void has a selection of reskinned grineer/corpus/infected characters to fight again in procedurally generated maps whilst derlict is the same maps as void but with some pathways block and a decayed looking void tileset. During the time I have played they have added tilesets for infected missions within the solar system and a pseudo null gravity environment, archwing. The have also added lots of weapons and warframes.The warframes are all human like with various elemental based abilities like WoW the weapons are either shotgun,rifle,pistol, melee with the first three firing either projectiles or "laser" beams. There are also 2 types of companion that you can take on your missions either sentenals or kubrow, sentenals are floating robots that have their own projectile weapon and the kubrow run along the ground biting things for damage. DE have recently added a "viable" PvP after many attempts over the time I have played and have gone a long way in clearing up a lot of the long standing bugs that would have put steam map makers to shame.
So Warframe on the good side is initially very pretty with a general WoW style to the player characters, if you liked dressing dollies as a child then you can customise your apperance futher with syandanas and helmets and colour pallete add ons. The play style is very much unreal tornament without the tornament about on a par with TF2 MvM, the game seemingly adds a wealth of weapon/frame/companion options but in reality there are minor differences beyond cosmetic between each items in those sets with variation of the items stats like damage type and rate of fire etc.
I used to play the WoW mod on Counterstrike and TF2 MvM and both were more enjoyable for a very simple reason, WF has very little player interaction.
If you look at the long running games then what they have in common was making and retaining groups of players, DE do not seems to understand this concept at all. I would say most players (IMHO 90%) get bored of the repetition after around 3-6 months and play something else instead, this has been the case since I started playing. DE have added locations where you can show off your warframe/weapons etc, they have added long missions that require coordination and still there is nothing in this game to bring people together by making friends. One of the worst things DE have done of late is censoring players in the tect chat threads, I understand some players can be offensive or annoying but the moderation ingame has become an increasing problem when you cannot vent your feelings after suffering lost time because of bad coding, in my experience posting a support ticket is a waste of time. After waiting weeks for support if they do reply then it is as though you wasted their time. I would not mind if I had not paid them cash during my time but investment is no promise of quality.

I recently came back to Warframe from a rather long hiatus, and WOW, the game is so much MORE now. If you played it a while ago, I really advise taking it out for another spin and getting hooked again!
This game is a little (grindy) gem, hidden here on Steam. But the grind is action packed, fun, and filled with tense moments of doubt. These challenges are overcome with skill and teamwork. This game is one of my favorite team/solo games. The missions have elements of CTF, Survival, Escort, Espionage and Exterminate/Assassinate, depending on the mission parameters. The different worlds offer variety, and the Archframe missions are a wanna-be mecha pilots joy.
Pro's-
-Amazing graphics, killing in space never looked so glorious!
-Fast paced gameplay, and fairly quick missions. Good for small or large time kill.
-Highly customizable gear by modding makes each player pretty unique.
-The boss fights are always a blast!
-Great community, join a guild right off for help and support! Teamwork is fun!
-Easy to pick up, takes some time and skill to master all the game has to offer.
-PvP is brutal, but I suspect once you get good at it a lot of fun.
-Space Ninja Mecha-madness!
Cons-
-Try to avoid running the same mission/world over and over, it can feel stale even while your reaping      rewards. Take advantage of the large variety of mission types and settings!
-Avoid buying gear from the Marketplace, the player Trade channel often has the same (or better) items for much, much less!

GameSpot's early access reviews evaluate unfinished games that are nonetheless available for purchase by the public. While the games in question are not considered finished by their creators, you may still devote money, time, and bandwidth for the privilege of playing them before they are complete. The review below critiques a work in progress, and represents a snapshot of the game at the time of the review's publication.
Like DayZ and H1Z1, ARK: Survival Evolved is another Early-Access survival game that has received an explosive amount of attention. But does it provide something different enough to warrant all the publicity? In short, no. You can collect materials, craft items, and tame dinosaurs, but many of those features are not exclusive to ARK, nor are they any better here. Serious functionality problems and lag exist, sapping enjoyment and crippling immersion. Still, it’s not completely awful. Given the chance, you can have a lot of fun, even if there are not many fresh ideas at this stage of development. The game can be entertaining at times and frustrating on occasion, but the evolution of survival it is not--at least not yet.

Excellent game overall. I have played hundreds of hours and this is the prettiest, most open world, most involving game I have ever played. Originally it was glitchy and buggy, but it has come a LONG WAY since early access. I have not played in 6 months, so I probably hardly recognize all the "finishing" touches they've put on the game. I play on a LAN server with my wife and we just try to survive against the environment, and the challenge with just a couple of us is still more than sufficient. In fact, this game really needs more people in many ways because boss battles are extremely difficult with just 1 or 2 people. Getting resources on the game's default settings is very labor and time intensive, and losing even a set of Flak armor can feel a bit frustrating.
.... As another reviewer mentioned, even with a top-of-the-line graphics card, this game challenges the system. I made my own server for this game. It runs at least 3.2 Gbs of RAM and will spike and increase until the server will run 10-12 Gbs of RAM!!! When I ran the server and the game simultaneously on my gaming PC (Core i7 2600K OC'd to 4.6 Ghz and GTX 1080) the server would crash the entire computer with memory errors. It would hog up all 16GB of DDR3-2400mhz RAM! and crash...
Now I moved the server to a Core-i3 (6th gen) with 16Gb of RAM (a $400 machine built mostly just for an Ark Server) and the server *rarely* crashes, but... still... on occassion... HOWEVER my GTX 1080 (the second best consumer graphics card in the WORLD at the time of writing) barely beats 30fps on Epic settings with a few features turned down, and the video drivers have crashed at least 1 time per day. Fortunately, I can usually kill my server and restart before a dinosaur finds my unconscious body and eats me!
This is a very fun game that is BEST played with a group of friends at NEAR the standard game settings. Turning up the games default resource gathering and leveling turns this into a nearly pointless sandbox without challenge, but the defaults I find to be a bit too much of a tedious slog. I think I finally decided on about a 25% boost in resources and leveling and a 25% reduction in the length of night for a two-player co-op LAN experience. What is great is that this game allows you to find your own preferences, and really play the way you want. I haven't played this in awhile, but I look forward to finding out all of the changes.

This game is♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Especially if you don't have enough money to buy a decent keyboard or microtransations.
Let's start from the beginning: The tutorial.
When i start the tutorial, i instantly find myself between two idiots shooting at me. So what's the first thing you do? Beat the crap out of them. So i run around and press all the buttons on my mouse aiming at their balls.
And my character just walked around, doing nothing. He didn't attack at all. He just took all the bullets like he had down syndrome. So i think "Maybe i have to get a weapon" and i look around for weapons. Died.
I retry, and this time i can see that there are no weapons here. I just kept taking bullets in the face helplessly, when right before i die, i see a TIIIINY text above the dudes' head.
Third try. I read the text with huge difficulty: "Press 1 to use power."
Really?
Freakin' 1?
To attack?
So i press 1 and he swings... something in the air, hitting nothing until i got REALLY close. So i killed them. In the end, i died two times and survived with 20% of health because of two dudes. AT THE TUTORIAL.
Since i was still confused about having to press 1 to attack in a third person shooter, i repeat, THIRD PERSON SHOOTER, i go to the options and search the keyboard bindings.
And i saw hell.
Left mouse button was not bind to shoot. It was bind to "Charge melee".
'E' was bind to USE melee. 'F' was to reload. Q was bind to the emoticons menu.
Are you serious? Are you for REAL? Like, now i scroll down and i find out that to interact with stuff i have to press, i dunno, X!
...Yes.
It was actually bind to the X button.
So after spending the longest time i ever had to spend to change the controls in a game, i... well, let's just skip to the part that i finish the tutorial, because it's useless.
So i get to the ship. And when the computer talks to me, i'm greeted with the worst English to Italian translation ever of what he says. Oh, and they're not subtitles. It's a tiiiiiny window on the left that disappears if i don't wear my glasses before he finishes talking. Not like what he said was important.
Second mission. (The tutorial counts as a mission because it doesn't explain anything and it's frustrating and useless.) I find out that the thing on my leg was installed by "The leader of the baddies". (I already saw that on the intro, but i thought it was mine and... whatever) So to find out what it does, i have to stealth to one of their data centers. Though i know it's probably controlling me.
And... well...♥♥♥♥♥♥ I actually liked this part. The parkour stuff was nice, and the dudes didn't have 360 degrees vision, like it should be. I liked the hacking part less, way, way too easy. And i got praised for not letting the alarm go when i got the data.
So it turns out the thing in my leg is trying to control me. OH MY GOD PLOT TWIST! WHAT A SURPRISE! THIS GAME IS SO ORIGINA- ok sorry.
Third mission. A dude that the baddies trapped has got... something to free my knee. So i kill the baddies, and THIS TIME the idiots got 360 vision. So i have to kill everyone and make me get revealed thousands of times. So i free the dude. The goal is to take the dude to the spaceship without letting him get killed. Easy, right?
Good freakin' luck, because he got Down syndrome.
One time he will run to the enemies to get killed, the other he will run in circles, the other he won't move at all, and at this point... I was too frustrated to continue.
I couldn't go on. I just couldn't. I was wasting time. A game should be made to be enjoyed during the very little spare time we have left. And this game wasted it.
Don't waste time and HDD space. Get Trove. Or Burnout. Get a FUN game.

What is great is that this game allows you to find your own preferences, and really play the way you want. I haven't played this in awhile, but I look forward to finding out all of the changes.

Warframe is a free-to-play, third-person, action shooter.
First off, I want to say that this game has one of the best monetization schemes I've ever seen in a F2P game -- where other games build their systems around getting players to spend money on stuff, and make letting players earn items by investing their time in the game be this difficult thing, Warframe feels like it was built with time investments as the primary expectation, and spending money second.
That is to say, a good 90% of the game's weapons, characters, and cosmetics can be earned and crafted without spending any money on the game, but spending money does allow one to gain access to them faster. The only things a player cannot earn are weapon and character slots, but these are reasonably priced.
Ostensibly, a player could even buy these slots without buying any of the game's premium currency because, at the moment, all trading can only be done for certain types of items (rare, high-end/late-game items and mods that cannot be bought from the premium store), and you cannot trade for credits, only premium currency. So one could earn a few of these items, sell them to other players, and use that premium currency to unlock more slots without spending a dime of their own money.
The game itself is fairly simple. There's a story, but it's in the background and really vague. You just go into missions, of which there are a variety of types and kill bad guys to get experience for you gear and character, materials to build new gear and characters, and mods to upgrade your gear and characters. You can play solo, but the game's scaling is generally geared towards multiple players. Matchmaking is easy and fluid (usually).
The way the game times the building of gear and characters combined with the rate at which you find the parts you need to build them means that once you get rolling, you can almost always have something new waiting to be leveled up, so there's a fairly constant sense of progression and growth, plus the fun of experimenting and figuring out the intricacies and tactical roles of each weapon and/or character.
There are a lot of bugs, some more significant than others, but the developer is constantly working to fix stuff. But their priorities are sometimes very different than their playerbase's.
All in all, I'd call it a 6/10 game. Nothing mind-blowingly awesome, but fun enough to sink time into, and an easy game to play when you want to kind of veg out, not worry about missing some critical plot point or something, if that makes any sense.

I used to have a joke review about how, having just under 1k hours, I was still considered a newb. Since ARK has finally launched from Early Access, I figured I should do an actual review for the game.
. I go over more of the mechanics in the video; this text review has a lot of complaints you’ll want to read if you’re deciding on the game or not.
ARK came onto the store after the disappointing Stomping Grounds became vaporware. Wildcard promised to provide a game where you could ride around on giant dinosaurs and conquer your enemies through sheer might. To a certain extent, they  made good on their promise. The first time you get a T-Rex as a pal and start to ride it around the map, you feel
. You can't start with a Rex though - While it's possible to knock one out and tame one, you have to level up enough to learn how to make a saddle - so you're encouraged to start small, with Dodos and Dilophosaurs.
That's the thing with ARK, though: It boasts a huge amount of creatures, close to 124 (not including the Alpha variants); the thing is, not all of these creatures feel particularly useful now. A good example would be a Parasaur, which, in the game, is described to have decent speed, high stamina, and be a fast swimmer. The latter isn't as true as it used to be, and the Parasaur is quickly outclassed by almost any other herbivore when it comes to harvesting or defense. They can't outrun early-game predators like a raptor, sabercat or direwolf, too.
Dinosaurs that were in the game during early access feel a little underwhelming compared to the recent additions. A great example is the Giganotosaurus, which dwarfs the T-Rex in size and damage output (an in-game dossier states the Rex is called the "Tyrannosaurs Dominum", because few "creatures on the Island can contest [it] for dominance").  It feels like Rexes are the only creatures from the first iteration of the game that are worthwhile… and judging by how end game revolves around them, they’re the only ones worth really investing time into in the long run.
The AI in ARK is still lacking. Certain carnivores, when aggro’d, immediately run
from you, only to run back after they’ve figured out whatever pathing problem they’ve had - or they just never come back, having run into (literally) another thing for them to attack. The pathing for tamed mounts is just as bad, with small, lightweight creatures over-exaggerating their turn radius while following you and flying off a cliff; or larger, slower creatures, whose turn radius is so wide that they have to be ridden through gates to be parked properly.
The fun part of ARK seems to be the beginning of the game, where you’re desperately trying to survive in an extremely harsh world. Overestimating yourself is often the downfall of any new ARK survivor, and sometimes the downfall of more experienced ones. There’s always a sense of fear when you play ARK in the beginning, even after building a small hut to house you and various goods you’ve acquired. After putting in enough time, you build enough defenses that you don’t feel as threatened, and the few deaths you experience are no longer a massive travesty, but just a mere annoyance.
And that’s when the grind kicks in.
A majority of the end game is grinding out resources to take on either the bosses of ARK, or to go into the Caves on whatever map you play on - the caves being ‘dungeons’ in typical games. However, taking your weapons into these areas means you have to make whatever ammo they need, and bullets are an expensive process; same for any type of handheld explosives. Your tames can help alleviate the grind, but with the amount of pressure put on getting the perfect tame, you also have to grind to get the appropriate eggs and rare foods to make the kibble your gathering creature prefers - also, kibble
reduces the amount of time it takes to tame your newly acquired mount, so you’ll just want it anyways.
Most of these can be sidestepped by joining a tribe that works together cohesively, but that takes making a big leap of faith and trusting strangers on your server if you haven’t brought friends along. To be honest, I really enjoyed that part of ARK - I still play with people I met on the first unofficial server I joined. For anyone that doesn’t want to deal with other people, I understand how much of a nightmare this sounds like: You either have to prepare yourself for a massive grind to take on end game content; you may have to join forces with people you don’t know; or you just might be forced onto one of the many unofficial servers with extremely boosted rates.
So this all sounds like I’m taking a massive crap on the game, but I actually really like ARK. Even with all of it’s flaws - which don’t get me wrong, there are
- it’s still a fun game to me. It appeals to a certain type of person. I do wish there were a lot more ways for lower-level players to properly combat the alpha tribes on their servers, but that status quo won’t change for a very long time.
If you aren’t a fan of survival games in general, you aren’t going to like ARK. If you love dinosaurs, but you can’t set aside your suspension of disbelief, you’ll hate the creature sin the game (all of which have had creative liberties taken with them). There’s not really much of a story until you’ve beaten all three bosses at least once, and even after decoding the scraps of information given to you, there’s not much in the way of true story. If you get upset when you lose things forever in video games, then do not get started in ARK.
But then there are these moments when you just barely make it out of a tough encounter; where either you or your tames leave with a battle with just a sliver of health; or a fight that’s won with your last rifle round; or even that feeling of pure happiness when one of your tames runs up to absolutely destroy whatever just knocked you out.
Those are the moments that I live for in ARK, and the moments I will always remember.
Overall, I give
a
- it’s flawed (and I can’t reiterate this enough), but can still be a very fun game to certain people.
If you’ve looked at any part of this review and gone “How can he give this a 7/10 with all these complaints?”, you aren’t going to like this game. That’s all there is to it. If you see any of the flashy videos Wildcard posts, especially of an upcoming expansion, and you’re thinking about buying it…
Just remember all of the complaints I have here. If any of them are enough to make second-guess your decision, you don’t want this game - expansion and all.

Alrighty! After 800 hours of logged playtime ( at the time of writing this review ) I think I have earned the right to review this game. I do not plan on overviewing the mechanics, or doing much in the way of an in depth review but hey I'll say what I think matters.

The game is entirely a grind for stronger and better-looking gear. The combat is undeniably fun and the graphics are beautiful, but the time gates and grind just make the game tedious to play.
Want a new weapon? Gotta buy the blueprint, grind out the resources, and then wait 12 hours for it to be built.
Want a new warframe? Gotta buy the blueprint, grind out the blueprints for the 3 separate parts in warframe's blueprint, and then grind out the resources for those parts and the original blueprint. Then wait 72 hours for it to get built.
That's essentially the entire game, there's no story or legitimate progression through the game, just grinding missions so you can craft better gear, so that you can grind even harder missions to craft even better gear.
OR you can buy any weapon or warframe fully ready from the Market for real money with no timegates or grinding. Hell you can even buy resources from the market, not to mention cosmetic items.
So your decision is to either spend 100s or 1000s of hours endlessly slaying enemies or spending $100s or $1000s of dollars to instantly unlock everything in the game.
If you like this type of grinding then you'll love the game, but for those who don't have the time or money to invest in than I wouldn't recommend playing this game too intently.

This means a lot of mindless grinding (most of the time you don't have to pay attention to enemies because they don't pose a threat). There's a real lack of "endgame" here. Think of it as Diablo III in space with more action and no leaderboards for end-tier players. Endgame consists of "how high can you go" Greater Rift-style runs.
Bottom Line:
- Entertainment for two-ish weeks
- Your character will look sweet if you put in effort/money
- Significant grind/time walls in place that try to lengthen out the experience
- You can buy almost everything with real money
- Most everything can be grinded given enough time/ luck
- Becomes mindless grind at a certain point

The bad part is that this game is Computer-Intensive.  When you log out your character doesn't leave, it just collapses right then and there so if your in a bad area, your gonna have a Bad Time.  Everything runs constantly (As can be expected of a online, persistent multiplayer world.) Which further means that logging off leaves you and your stuff/base/dinos at risk. Perhaps the biggest deciding factor for some will be the Requirements.  This game does not like mid to low end computers. Some claim this is because the Devs have not properly Optimized and instead focused on more content (Such as the above mentioned DLC) . I truely hope that Optimization happens soon, because it has alot of good going for it.  And for those who like mods, there are plenty of mod-oriented servers who will spoonfeed you each mod they require instead of making you hunt it down, so its got that going for it!
Overall: 7/10 - Dinos are well animated, if not perfectly, enviroments are nice as well as big, but require a strong computer to be able to properly appreciate. Now before I start, without a doubt yes I would recommend this game.
Now, for the meat of it. Ark: Survival Evolved has a lot of aspects that a fantastic survival open world game should have. We have base construction, simplistic food and drink systems, base stamina with no need to sleep, and the ability to tame the wild and use them as you see fit. This on its own is fantastic and I've had countless hours of fun doing so.
However; the sheer fact that Wildcard decided scortched earth was a good idea and to cross some servers via the Arks is probably the worst decision possible. They took time and effort that could be used to polish the main game and put it into some half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥stand alone version. Not to mention that you can bring creatures that were never balanced for the Survival Evolved client and use them to create untold problems, I'm looking at you Wyverns. These flying minge beasts are exponentially stronger used on a Survival evolved server, not to mention rock golems.
In closing, if you choose to play this game do so on a server that doesn't have cross game play. Save yourself hours of frustration and enjoy the relatively clear skies.

Then the real game begins as you watch hundreds of hours of your hard work be destroyed in a matter of seconds. Without any emotion you'll get up from your cold dark basement bedroom and walk out the front door for the first time in months. -Game is very glitchy. It also gets extremely unstable for a good week or so after updates.
-Some praise how the game isn't P2W, but it sure seems that the RNG greatly favors those who constantly waste their money on the game. Hard to prove, but not outlandish. Especially when all F2P games are founded on scamming their playerbase (unfortunate fact, I know. Look it up).
Besides the various lacking areas of the game itself, the fanboys are by far the biggest drag. You know the type, regardless of the action, the game is absolutely perfect and the developers can do no wrong.
I know I'm forgetting a ton of stuff, but it really doesn't matter. Go ahead and try it, it's fun for awhile, but I greatly advise that you save your money and get out before you get too invested.

Warframe is a unique game in its design and way you play. Ive played just under 100 hours and ive found its mostly one playstyle or playtype, horde.
Warframe has a few major gametypes but the best one is survival(basically horde like gears of war) warframe doesnt have much story development to speak of, however there is some pretty interesting lore to explore on certain warframes. Expect to grind quite a bit, and even wait days for your built items to be finished unless you buy platinum to either rush projects or buy them outright on the market. But as ive played world of warcraft since it first came out almost a decade ago i really dont mind the grindy nature of this game because its so enjoyable and doesnt seem pointless while your playing it. Everything you do in warframe has a purpose and the chance for something great to happen.
Also warframe has an amazingly well made co-op system that is seamlessly intigrated into the playing experience. If your friend want to drop in during battle its simply one click away and you guys are together. And speaking of co-operative experience, the "clans" or guilds for wow players, are amazing. Everything that you would have ever wanted from a massive clan to have a badass headquarters can be built in warframe. If you dont believe me youtube some of the labyrinth clan "dojos" (thats what the headquarters are called). Literally so huge you can easily get lost in them and every single door, every wall can be customized in almost every way possible. You start off with a single room, and build from there until you have 60+ rooms on 20+ floors with elevators its amazing. Plus in your dojo you can build weapons, warframes, gear and mods that are actually effective and even better than what you could buy with real money.
But if there is anything warframe has to offer its an amazing fighting system that is incredibly diverse and customizable. Possibly the best parkour and movement abilities implimented seamlessly into a game ive ever played. The fighting system is extremely fun and engaging, and the enemies may not be very different from one another, they are sufficiently diverse so that you know what your killing and what works against certain factions.
However, warframe also has a PVP system called conclave. Ive found this gameplay mode to be pretty fun, and extremely fast paced. I didnt dive too deep into the pvp system yet, but from what ive played its fun.
And last of all ive found that the balance in warframe is near perfect, its far from pay to play as you can actually acquire everything in the game from just playing it. And while you can buy a much better starting weapon right off the bat if you buy platinum, the best weapons in the game cannot be bought and they must be attained through farming/building. The warframes themselves are well balanced, arguably the best warframes in the entire game are two of the first three that you can pick from in the starting set excalibur and mag making this extremely well balanced.
All in all, warframe is free to play done right. It offers amazing graphics, a battle system that is diverse and extremely customizable to your play style and a movement/parkour system that is so seamless you wonder how you have played without it.

This game entertained me for an entire summer and I have only just recently started to get bored with it. And that is simply because I am burned out on it. The gameplay is very fun, taking the route of "Badass overpowered space ninja kills everything in sight". The game is very invigorating to play and is interesting to explore and learn about it's history and storyline. There are 5 factions in Warframe as of this review; The Corpus, The Grineer, The Corrupted, The Infested, and of course the Tenno. The Corpus are a group of war merchants, specializing in robotic proxy's. The Corpus do not care who buys their goods, only about profit. They have a hatred for the Tenno due to their crimes against the long dead Orokin (now the Corrupted). As well as worshipping the Orokin and their technology. The Grineer are a powerhouse of clones hell bent on nothing but conquering the Origin System. They are the first enemy faction encountered by the player. The Corrupted are a combination of corpus, grineer, and infested enemies all contaminated by the corrupted AI. Their only purpose is to defend the Orokin Towers they reside in. The infested are the incarnation of the Tecnoctye Virus which was a main plot device in Warframe's precursor; Dark Sector. The Tenno are the faction controlled by the player. Not much is known, most players do not care. Personally I believe the Orokin created the Warframe during the dark war. An infamous conflict between the Orokin and the Sentients (both canonically wiped out by the Tenno). The Tenno were Orokin which were exposed to the Void's energy. Twisting them into unpredictable reactors of energy. All within the same minute a single Tenno without it's Frame could; light the air on fire, freeze the moisture in the air, spread iron across it's skin, heal wounds, turn invisible, control one's mind, etc. The Orokin, in desperation, turned to these Tenno and built the Warframes around them to control and channel their unpredictable abilities into certain areas. I believe that it took only the first experimental Tenno to destroy the Sentients. After which the Tenno were forced into a life of slavery and dirty work. Until a rougue Orokin female, The Lotus. Advised the Tenno and informed them of their strength. And convinced them to destroy their false idols. (Theorized). The Tenno were being honored by the Orokin with ten beats of a drum, a horified Orokin realized that the Tenno had ill intent. He watched as on the ninth beat of the drum, the Tenno slaughtered the Orokin council. The Orokin citizen watching was spared and became the vengeful Stalker, an assassin which will target Tenno who have slain a boss. The Tenno then went on to threaten the Corpus, who scolded them but refused to oppose them. The Grineer also refused to oppose the mighty warrior gods. The Tenno then slept in cryosleep for an untold number of years. This is where my ranting ends as the Tenno's awakening is the end of the Dark Sector storyline. Warframe has no real story, only lore. This game is full of farming, and has pay to win elements. These elements are easily worked around through hard work and trading, however. Overall, I love this game and give it an 8/10

I currently have 2,837hrs recorded on this game, all on a primitive PVP server.  Even though player combat is severely outdated the majority of the game is really addicting.  I enjoy the crafting, taming, breeding, building the most as combat really needs to be updated for true PVP to be enjoyable.  The game itself steadily improves with most patches but is unfortunately plagued by the SE Expansion.  Let's start with some of the good from a Primitive PVP server view as these servers focus more on the dinos.
The Crafting and building system still needs work but even in its basic form is addicting.  You can never have too much defense(more on that later) and some players can still make amazing looking buildings with the limited items you have to craft with.  Crafting takes time but once you get a system down for farming materials you mass produce structures and build build build.  Unfortunately you will hit a point that your base causes the game to freeze up for a moment when rendering in slowly.
Taming and Breeding are a huge part of Primitive as everything you do relies heavily on the Dinos that you have aquired.  Taming can take insane amounts of time out of your day and you really are forced into going for the strongest possible if you plan to survive.   The long tame times may seem horrible but if they were shorter then you would likely see more trolls aquiring stronger pets.  Breeding is actually really simple, however many seem to make it seem complex.  Breed to get the best stats all mixed into 1 to gain overpowered dinos.
Combat is rather lacking.  Hit detection is way off with melee, ranged seems to have a slight delay, and dino combat is generally boring with just 1 bit animation over and over and over.  The real joy in combat is defeating an enemy but otherwise is a bit of a bore.
The major negatives with the current state of the game.  Up until now it was possible to stop constant trolling especially from online streamers by defeating the players, knocking them out, and caging them.  They were a plague but they did bring some excitement to the servers as it caused the community to team up and defeat them.  Unfortunately the paid expansion was released even with the game being in Alpha which is a problem of its own.  This expansion has caused multiple balance issues with the game and has made it not worth playing on PVP servers.
Fire arrows seem like a small item but they are currently overpowered.  Players can mass produce these from a number of servers, transport to an The Island and easily wipe out any dino that is exposed or simply pick open a wall and wipe big dinos in minutes.  The issue is the damage per shot is way too high for the cheap cost of the arrows.  The streamers love this as it now takes little skill to kill big dinos that would usually require an equal or stronger dino to defeat.  A simple nerf to damage would easily resolve this huge issue but it still has not been patched.
One-sided server transfers.  Now I understand this is by design to get more players to feel the need to purchase the expansion but it has caused a severe balance issue.  Players on The Island can only be on the defensive now.  There is no true way to strike back at your attackers as they can come from many different servers and Island dwellers can only transfer their naked bodies to fight back.  All The Island can do is sit and wait.  This has caused loot drops to be blocked and the obelisks to be built over to slow down this issue however it cannot stop it.  One night while you sleep a foreign streamer can bring over an entire army of Elementals and Wyverns and lock out the server with their viewers logging in to prevent players from even defending their own server.
Unfortunately this game breaking tactic has made Official PVP servers not worth the effort as it's just a matter of time until this plague comes to your server.  I have yet to lose anything to these streamers and their tactics however that cannot be said for many others.  Even with all the time I have in the game I will be leaving the Official servers as it's not worth the time to defend knowing that I cannot ever be on offense.   I recommend sticking to private servers or PVE until the Devs look at these major balance issues that have been created with this paid Expansion.  Ark itself I can recommend but PVP servers while tied to an Expansion server I cannot recommend at this time.

ARK: Survival Evolved is a game with GREAT potential; however it is also a game that tends to frustrate it's fanbase.
I struggled for a while to decide on whether to give this game a positive recommendation or not; in the end, I decided to fall on the side of 'positive' because I see all that it can be, given time.
Now, the thing that fans of this game tend to forget (myself included, at times) is that it's still very much in an Alpha state.  For those that aren't familiar with that phrase, for whatever reason, a referesher: A game in Alpha is at it's earliest stages of development.  Not all the content is there; new content is being constantly added. Bugs *will* be rampant. A game in it's Beta stage has had all the base content included, and the focus now switches to fixing glitches and bugs before full, final release.
For a game in Alpha, ARK: SE *is* very far along. There are a large number of dinosaurs to tame (the devs are actually approaching the end of the list as far as initial dinos they wanted in the game), the visuals are all there and gorgeous, even on a rig that can only run it at medium-high levels (lower levels not so much, as would be expected), there's hundreds of craftables present in game and all of them serve a purpose, even if said purpose is just for roleplaying, such as the Wardrums.  I've often told friends not aware of the game's existence that it's 'essentially Minecraft with better graphics and tameable/ridable dinosaurs'.  There's also a number of maps, both official and unofficial, to play on, and now that the environment biomes have been introduced, they're even more fleshed out (my personal favorite is still the base 'Island' map though..but this means I miss out on the wicked cool Wyvern, which is only present in the Scorched Earth paid DLC unless you use mods or admin-power cheats).
One of the aspects that I'm a huge fan of is the fact that there are both official servers as well as unofficial. Personally, I feel the base rates for tame times, harvest rates, and XP gain are rather a bit low (seriously, who has the time to spend *2 hours* taming a mere level 1 Brontosaurus using the standard methods?) The base rates lend themselves towards a certain lack of fluidity in progression; many of the available dinos in game offer some kind of perk or benefit to make other things in game easier, but in order to tame those dinosaurs efficiently, you need to have progressed far enough to be able to craft and obtain the weapons and foods to make the taming process time efficient, which sometimes means you're at a level where you no longer need the benefit the dino you want to tame provides, because you've already gotten that benefit just from reaching a high enough level.  For example: one of the newest tames added, the Diplocaulus, is an amphibian that has air bladders in its head.  If you take this tame underwater, it has the effect of increasing your available oxygen, at the cost of it's own.  This makes deep sea diving and exploration feasible, since it's also a relatively speedy mound.  However, to tame it in the fastest manner possible, you need to feed it a certain type of kibble, made from a combination of berries, jerky, and Archaeopteryx eggs.  The easiest way to get the most-difficult-find ingredient, the eggs, is to find and tame a mated pair of Archy's.  However, Archy's are so rare that by the time you find both a male and female, and preferably multiple females to actually make an egg 'farm' (and then have enough eggs to make enough kibble for the Diplocaulus tame), you're likely at or close to level 75 anyway, when SCUBA gear becomes available, making the Diplo unnecessary. Playing on an Unofficial server with boosted rates balances this out, by making the tame time using the basic method (raw meat, in the case of the Diplo, which is dropped by all of the land animals in game) much more feasible, and negating the need to make it feasible by kibble; in these cases kibble just makes the tame SUPER fast (and adding the most amount of levels on tame, if you care about that sort of thing.)  And if you decide to run your own server, either from your own rig or by renting server space from a number of host sites online, you can set rates yourself, as well as a number of other settings to optimize your play experience, including selecting which dinos you want available and how often they spawn, the day/night ratio and speed of the passing of in game time, the amount of time it takes to breed dinos from eggs (a recently added feature) and how much time the baby spends in each stage of development until it reaches adulthood,  and much more.
Now, as I said earlier, there are still plenty of bugs and glitches in this game.  AI and pathing for dino's can be somewhat wonky (don't even get me started on how spastic Pteranodon's can be), glitching into the ground is somewhat common, which can be infuriating when trying to locate your corpse to reacquire inventory you don't want to lose, there are well known issues with certain spawns being broken on unofficial servers (the last one I played on that I wasn't running myself had Quetzal spawns completely broken; the only way to get one was by the admin spawning them in forcibly and then attempting to tame as normal), and certain unofficial servers have had issues where data wipes itself and the server has to be either rolled back to a previous date, or wiped completely, both of which result in a tremendous loss of progress.  But again, this is an *Alpha state game*; these things are to be expected, and if you pay for this and then expect perfection, you're rather a fool.
The biggest grievance players have right now is the fact that the game is still in Alpha, and the developers are releasing paid DLC.  I can understand both sides of this issue; gamers don't want to pay for extra content when the base content is still being worked on, and the developers feel the need to recoup losses from their recent legal troubles.  However, I feel if the devs wanted to maintain trust, they'd eventually make back their losses simply by devoting time into developing ARK into a finished product which would then rather sell itself.  But as is fairly well known in the industry these days, the focus is on making as much money short term as possible, which leads to situations like the one ARK is in where it actually loses a lot of its fanbase by concentrating on short term goals, rather than long term ones.
All in all, ARK: Survival Evolved *is* a game worth paying for, offering hundreds upon hundreds of hours of fun and socialization, and is well worth the $30 ($15 at the moment, being on sale) you'd pay for it.  We, as gamers, just have to remember it is still firmly in it's infancy, and shouldn't expect $60 quality from something still in such an early stage.

ARK: Survival Evolved is a game with GREAT potential; however it is also a game that tends to frustrate it's fanbase.
I struggled for a while to decide on whether to give this game a positive recommendation or not; in the end, I decided to fall on the side of 'positive' because I see all that it can be, given time.
Now, the thing that fans of this game tend to forget (myself included, at times) is that it's still very much in an Alpha state.  For those that aren't familiar with that phrase, for whatever reason, a referesher: A game in Alpha is at it's earliest stages of development.  Not all the content is there; new content is being constantly added. Bugs *will* be rampant. A game in it's Beta stage has had all the base content included, and the focus now switches to fixing glitches and bugs before full, final release.
For a game in Alpha, ARK: SE *is* very far along. There are a large number of dinosaurs to tame (the devs are actually approaching the end of the list as far as initial dinos they wanted in the game), the visuals are all there and gorgeous, even on a rig that can only run it at medium-high levels (lower levels not so much, as would be expected), there's hundreds of craftables present in game and all of them serve a purpose, even if said purpose is just for roleplaying, such as the Wardrums.  I've often told friends not aware of the game's existence that it's 'essentially Minecraft with better graphics and tameable/ridable dinosaurs'.  There's also a number of maps, both official and unofficial, to play on, and now that the environment biomes have been introduced, they're even more fleshed out (my personal favorite is still the base 'Island' map though..but this means I miss out on the wicked cool Wyvern, which is only present in the Scorched Earth paid DLC unless you use mods or admin-power cheats).
One of the aspects that I'm a huge fan of is the fact that there are both official servers as well as unofficial. Personally, I feel the base rates for tame times, harvest rates, and XP gain are rather a bit low (seriously, who has the time to spend *2 hours* taming a mere level 1 Brontosaurus using the standard methods?) The base rates lend themselves towards a certain lack of fluidity in progression; many of the available dinos in game offer some kind of perk or benefit to make other things in game easier, but in order to tame those dinosaurs efficiently, you need to have progressed far enough to be able to craft and obtain the weapons and foods to make the taming process time efficient, which sometimes means you're at a level where you no longer need the benefit the dino you want to tame provides, because you've already gotten that benefit just from reaching a high enough level.  For example: one of the newest tames added, the Diplocaulus, is an amphibian that has air bladders in its head.  If you take this tame underwater, it has the effect of increasing your available oxygen, at the cost of it's own.  This makes deep sea diving and exploration feasible, since it's also a relatively speedy mound.  However, to tame it in the fastest manner possible, you need to feed it a certain type of kibble, made from a combination of berries, jerky, and Archaeopteryx eggs.  The easiest way to get the most-difficult-find ingredient, the eggs, is to find and tame a mated pair of Archy's.  However, Archy's are so rare that by the time you find both a male and female, and preferably multiple females to actually make an egg 'farm' (and then have enough eggs to make enough kibble for the Diplocaulus tame), you're likely at or close to level 75 anyway, when SCUBA gear becomes available, making the Diplo unnecessary. Playing on an Unofficial server with boosted rates balances this out, by making the tame time using the basic method (raw meat, in the case of the Diplo, which is dropped by all of the land animals in game) much more feasible, and negating the need to make it feasible by kibble; in these cases kibble just makes the tame SUPER fast (and adding the most amount of levels on tame, if you care about that sort of thing.)  And if you decide to run your own server, either from your own rig or by renting server space from a number of host sites online, you can set rates yourself, as well as a number of other settings to optimize your play experience, including selecting which dinos you want available and how often they spawn, the day/night ratio and speed of the passing of in game time, the amount of time it takes to breed dinos from eggs (a recently added feature) and how much time the baby spends in each stage of development until it reaches adulthood,  and much more.
Now, as I said earlier, there are still plenty of bugs and glitches in this game.  AI and pathing for dino's can be somewhat wonky (don't even get me started on how spastic Pteranodon's can be), glitching into the ground is somewhat common, which can be infuriating when trying to locate your corpse to reacquire inventory you don't want to lose, there are well known issues with certain spawns being broken on unofficial servers (the last one I played on that I wasn't running myself had Quetzal spawns completely broken; the only way to get one was by the admin spawning them in forcibly and then attempting to tame as normal), and certain unofficial servers have had issues where data wipes itself and the server has to be either rolled back to a previous date, or wiped completely, both of which result in a tremendous loss of progress.  But again, this is an *Alpha state game*; these things are to be expected, and if you pay for this and then expect perfection, you're rather a fool.
The biggest grievance players have right now is the fact that the game is still in Alpha, and the developers are releasing paid DLC.  I can understand both sides of this issue; gamers don't want to pay for extra content when the base content is still being worked on, and the developers feel the need to recoup losses from their recent legal troubles.  However, I feel if the devs wanted to maintain trust, they'd eventually make back their losses simply by devoting time into developing ARK into a finished product which would then rather sell itself.  But as is fairly well known in the industry these days, the focus is on making as much money short term as possible, which leads to situations like the one ARK is in where it actually loses a lot of its fanbase by concentrating on short term goals, rather than long term ones.
All in all, ARK: Survival Evolved *is* a game worth paying for, offering hundreds upon hundreds of hours of fun and socialization, and is well worth the $30 ($15 at the moment, being on sale) you'd pay for it.  We, as gamers, just have to remember it is still firmly in it's infancy, and shouldn't expect $60 quality from something still in such an early stage.

In all honesty, ARK is a very hard game to get into.  Obviously the game isn't finished yet, and at this rate, it might not be finished until 2020.  I've never been able to spend more than an hour at a time playing the game due to the buggy, clunky, and choppy experience that comes with it.  I have an intel i7 running at 4Ghz, with 16 GB of Ram, and a GTX 1070, and unfortunately ARK still doesn't run very well.  Not only is the game poorly optimized to this day, it doesn't appear to be getting the T.L.C. that it so desperately needs.  Steam says I've spent 6 hours in game, but I've actually put about 12 hours into the game.
I'd love to give a full review of the game, but the game loses all of its luster within a few hours of slogging through the muddled gameplay and unintuitive user interface.  The real shame is that I would really like to be able to get into ARK, because the ideas and imagination is all there and ARK does show a huge amount of potential.  As it stands though this game has been very disappointing, even in early access, which is odd considering the game is updated at least every other day.  The updates however, rarely include any improvements to gameplay performance or the UI.
Perhaps I'll reinstall ARK when the game is finished in a year, or two... or three, or four.  Until then, I'm going to use the 50Gb of space that this puppy takes up for games that I'll spend more time playing and enjoying.

Space Ninjas. Sold.
Honestly though, once you can get past the overall grind for items built into the game, there is a whole lot of really wonderful stuff to experience.
The look is great. The combat and gun-play is great. The movement and speed of gameplay is great. The customizability of everything you own is just downright awesome, and the use of mods on all your weapons and warframes makes for some very serious changes to your potential playstyle.
Free to play done correctly. The only things that cannot be gained through gameplay are pretty much cosmetic, and additional weapon/frame slots once you start to build up an inventory. Although spending real monies unlocking things can be done, the whole community is actually very supportive of the idea that doing that is "wasteful", since as the game progresses, unlocking weapons and new warframes becomes easier.
I would say it took me a good 2-4 hours to get settings and become familiar with the gameplay and mechanics. Things started to get a lot more enjoyable once over that hurdle. Over 24 hours in, still on my first warframe, have a few different weapons and having a good time running fast-paced missions with others from the community.

This not a review, but how to make a delicios Souffle.
INGREDIENTS
Unsalted butter, room temperature, for baking dish
1/4 cup sugar, plus more for baking dish
8 ounces semisweet chocolate, finely chopped, or semisweet chocolate chips (1 cup)
1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 large egg yolks, lightly beaten, plus 4 large egg whites
1/4 teaspoon cream of tartar
METHOD
Preheat oven to 350 degrees. Lightly butter a 1 1/2-quart tall-sided baking dish. Coat with sugar, tapping out excess. Set dish on a rimmed baking sheet.
In a large heatproof bowl set over a pot of simmering water, combine chocolate, vanilla, and 1/4 cup water. Stir until chocolate is melted and mixture is smooth, about 10 minutes. Remove from heat and let cool to room temperature, 20 minutes.
Stir egg yolks into cooled chocolate mixture until well combined. Set souffle base aside.
In a large bowl, using an electric mixer, beat egg whites and cream of tartar on medium-high until soft peaks form, about 2 minutes. Gradually add sugar and beat until stiff, glossy peaks form, about 5 minutes (do not overbeat).
In two additions, fold egg-white mixture into souffle base: With a rubber spatula, gently cut down through center and lift up some base from bottom of bowl. Turning bowl, steadily continue to cut down and lift up base until just combined.
Transfer mixture to dish, taking care not to get batter on top edge of dish; smooth top. Bake souffle until puffed and set, 30 to 35 minutes. (Do not open oven during first 25 minutes of baking.) Serve immediately.

Ah, Warframe. Where do I begin? I started playing Warframe a few days after the launch of Update 9 (that's back when Nova first came out), and since then the game has basically changed in every way. From Parkour to Damage, we've seen it all (except stealth, but I'll get to that later. I'll give a short version of my review and a long version. Short first.
_________________________________
Intro:
Warframe is a unique 3rd Person Shooter that combines elements of your average third person shooter with a twist: Character abilities and a "mod" mechanic, allowing you to essentially play whatever Warframe you want, however you want. Deep combat and customization (not physical customization).
THE GOOD:
- The unique "mod" mechanic makes for very deep and thought provoking gameplay and combat, and with the right mindset you can build Warframes to utilise certain abilities, weapons, or gameplay styles.
- Fun combat! Who cares about depth when it isn't fun?
- A Warframe for just about everyone!
- Good Customer Support
THE BAD:
- Only 2-3 weapons per category are viable for use in the end-game, as well as certain Warframe's abilities being rendered useless at the infinitely scaling enemy health bar.
- Good weapons tend to get put in then quickly destroyed via nerfs, and in wanting to allow weapon diversity, it reduces viable weapons to the 2-3 mentioned.
- Most Weapons and Warframes are hidden behind several layers of RNG, causing some Warframes to be nigh unattainable unless you trade for them via real world money's worth of an in-game currency
Overall: This game has many issues. MANY, many issues. It's fun at the end of the day, but albeit, very frustrating at times. I'd say give it a play.
Intro:
Warframe is a unique 3rd Person Shooter that combines elements of your average third person shooter with a twist: Character abilities and a "mod" mechanic, allowing you to essentially play whatever Warframe you want, however you want. Deep combat and customization (not physical customization).
That basically sums up the good. The game is very fun, despite all of its flaws. Which I will point out.
[NOTE: These issues could be resolved in the coming weeks, months, or years. Research for yourself unless you're seeing this before Update 18+]
THE BAD:
Warframe's end-game roster is very limited, and despite efforts to make other weapons worth using to increase diversity, most of what they do is nerf. Not just any nerf, but destroy. Weapons, anyway. Warframe balancing is awesome (although how Mesa has not been nerfed yet is beyond me). In trying to increase the roster, they have managed to wittle down what's worth using in total to about
. All of which are locked down behind many walls of RNG. Every time a weapon worthy of use in the Meta is released, it is quickly shoved back into the "NO META FOR YOU" box, effectively removing perfectly good weapons, weapons you spend real money on and lots of time on, might I add, and making them utterly useless. Beware, fellow Tenno.
And don't even get me started on stealth. It's nonexistant. Empty. A shell of something amazing. Cake without yeast. It's that kind of mess. Same goes for Archwing. And Sharkwing. Same deal.
The majority of the elements feel half-a**ed, and thrown in for the sake of a reminder to finish them later, else they'd quickly forget the idea in the first place. Not that that's not what's happening right now, that is.
Mods: You've heard the good. Here's the bad. Some mods are nearly impossible to get, and harder to rank. It takes an incredible amount of work to do. Not only that, but they constantly "fix" locations that will allow us to gear ourselves at some point in this lifetime by being the most efficient with Fusion Cores, XP, and resources (slight hyperbole;
). Not to mention those hard-to-get mods are the best ones. The ones absolutely necessary for the end-game. You will not be successful without them. Period.
They never nerf weapons well, as nerfs always destroy weapons, and buffs are needed for many things but are rarely ever seen. Again, buffs are seen on Warframes just as much as nerfs. Warframes are balanced, weapons are not.
My biggest issue with this game is their tendency to take perfectly viable weapons and mods (ones not on the 11 roster of viable weapons), and beat them to a pulp and throw them away, spitting in the face of anyone who put work into it. You can always make more money... but you can never get more time... days and days of work, all for naught at the press of a few keys by the devs. Be careful in what you craft. Wait a LONG time before you craft it. Make sure it won't get nerfed, and you won't get burned. Like I have many times.
This game is worth playing, but it has many core issues that need to be fixed to keep people coming back. It's no coincidence more veteran players are leaving with each day, and they're losing players just as much as gaining new ones. It's this mentality of f*cking over experienced players and rewarding noobs, and nerfing to oblivion that will ultimately ruin this game if it isn't addressed. Play it while it's here.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding cheese cake recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1 cup digestive plain sweet biscuit crumbs
3 tablespoons sugar
3 tablespoons melted butter
40 ounces softened cream cheese
1 cup sugar
3 tablespoons flour
1 tablespoon vanilla
1 cup sour cream
4 eggs
Directions:
For The base:.
If you're using a dark pan, preheat the oven to 350. If you are using a shiny pan, 375.
Combine the crumbs, melted butter and 3 tbsp sugar well and pat onto the bottom of a 9 inch springform pan. I also like to very very lightly butter the sides of the pan so that the cheesecake will not stick later on.
Bake for 10 mins in your preheated oven and remove. Let it cool while you prepare your batter.
For the batter:.
Make sure everything is at room temperature.
Combine sugar, cheese, flour and vanilla in a big bowl and mix on medium speed till well combined. Don't forget to scrape the bowl as you're doing this.
Mix in the sour cream till its incorporated well. Then, add the eggs one by one, mixing well after each addition.
Pour the batter into the springform and let it bake for 1 hour and 10 minutes After the baking time, turn off the oven and leave the door ajar. Let the cake cool in there for about 1 1/2 hours.
Remove the cake and let it cool thoroughly. Refrigerate overnight.
Release the sides of the springform.
Eat.

INGREDIENTS
Unsalted butter, room temperature, for baking dish
1/4 cup sugar, plus more for baking dish
8 ounces semisweet chocolate, finely chopped, or semisweet chocolate chips (1 cup)
1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 large egg yolks, lightly beaten, plus 4 large egg whites
1/4 teaspoon cream of tartar
METHOD
Preheat oven to 350 degrees. Lightly butter a 1 1/2-quart tall-sided baking dish. Coat with sugar, tapping out excess. Set dish on a rimmed baking sheet.
In a large heatproof bowl set over a pot of simmering water, combine chocolate, vanilla, and 1/4 cup water. Stir until chocolate is melted and mixture is smooth, about 10 minutes. Remove from heat and let cool to room temperature, 20 minutes.
Stir egg yolks into cooled chocolate mixture until well combined. Set souffle base aside.
In a large bowl, using an electric mixer, beat egg whites and cream of tartar on medium-high until soft peaks form, about 2 minutes. Gradually add sugar and beat until stiff, glossy peaks form, about 5 minutes (do not overbeat).
In two additions, fold egg-white mixture into souffle base: With a rubber spatula, gently cut down through center and lift up some base from bottom of bowl. Turning bowl, steadily continue to cut down and lift up base until just combined.
Transfer mixture to dish, taking care not to get batter on top edge of dish; smooth top. Bake souffle until puffed and set, 30 to 35 minutes. (Do not open oven during first 25 minutes of baking.) Serve immediately.

So, what to say about Ark. I bought this game about two weeks ago and i've put very nearly 100 hours into the game so far. I must say that I was pleasantly suprised with the amount of content the game allows, especially for an early access title. Progression in game is a bit tedious for first time players, until you make a bed and get get your bearings, then it starts to level out. Maybe the first 20 hours of my experience was spent playing alone, the rest was spending time with 2 of my friends in game and starting a tribe, and that is where the best parts of this game are hidden. Co-op is an absolute gem, and teaming up on large dinos is just so rewarding. The only downfall really is dealing with more experienced players. In a game like this, it is more than expected to deal with some griefers, and in a strange way its part of the fun. However, if you are unlucky enough to hit the wrong server, you could have most of the server harassing you once you start to gather early to mid game resources. Having to start over before you've even got much of a foothold is difficult and beyond frustrating, but as long as you test the waters of the server before you commit to one, you should be fine.
With a decent rig, the game plays smooth on medium settings. High graphics were just the biggest pain, but even on medium it looks pretty solid. The draw distance isn't the best, and for some reason at a distance I can see mademade structures hidden behind large rocks before I could see the rocks, although that is more of a nitpick than anything. There is the occasional rubber banding, particularly on the water and when riding dinos, and you'll see some creatures stuck in rocks and trees, but aside from those minor issues, there arent many glitches.
Overall I have only 2 large grievances with the game. First, transfering your survivor from one official server to another doesn't work, and you need Scorched Earth to transfer at all, which is a big no no in my book. Secondly, it updates every damn day, and there seems to be no improvements, so I'm really not sure why they do it. Considering that it is an early access game, it's put together very well, and it is worth your time if you dig survival games in general. If you don't, I would still recommend it, just start on a PvE server to get the hang of it before you jump into PvP. I have not tried Scorched Earth yet, and although I disagree with their decision to put out paid DLC before they finished the base game, I still enjoy the game and will be sure to put more hours in.

So, what to say about Ark. I bought this game about two weeks ago and i've put very nearly 100 hours into the game so far. I must say that I was pleasantly suprised with the amount of content the game allows, especially for an early access title. Progression in game is a bit tedious for first time players, until you make a bed and get get your bearings, then it starts to level out. Maybe the first 20 hours of my experience was spent playing alone, the rest was spending time with 2 of my friends in game and starting a tribe, and that is where the best parts of this game are hidden. Co-op is an absolute gem, and teaming up on large dinos is just so rewarding. The only downfall really is dealing with more experienced players. In a game like this, it is more than expected to deal with some griefers, and in a strange way its part of the fun. However, if you are unlucky enough to hit the wrong server, you could have most of the server harassing you once you start to gather early to mid game resources. Having to start over before you've even got much of a foothold is difficult and beyond frustrating, but as long as you test the waters of the server before you commit to one, you should be fine.
With a decent rig, the game plays smooth on medium settings. High graphics were just the biggest pain, but even on medium it looks pretty solid. The draw distance isn't the best, and for some reason at a distance I can see mademade structures hidden behind large rocks before I could see the rocks, although that is more of a nitpick than anything. There is the occasional rubber banding, particularly on the water and when riding dinos, and you'll see some creatures stuck in rocks and trees, but aside from those minor issues, there arent many glitches.
Overall I have only 2 large grievances with the game. First, transfering your survivor from one official server to another doesn't work, and you need Scorched Earth to transfer at all, which is a big no no in my book. Secondly, it updates every damn day, and there seems to be no improvements, so I'm really not sure why they do it. Considering that it is an early access game, it's put together very well, and it is worth your time if you dig survival games in general. If you don't, I would still recommend it, just start on a PvE server to get the hang of it before you jump into PvP. I have not tried Scorched Earth yet, and although I disagree with their decision to put out paid DLC before they finished the base game, I still enjoy the game and will be sure to put more hours in.

Ah, Warframe. Where do I begin? I started playing Warframe a few days after the launch of Update 9 (that's back when Nova first came out), and since then the game has basically changed in every way. From Parkour to Damage, we've seen it all (except stealth, but I'll get to that later. I'll give a short version of my review and a long version. Short first.
_________________________________
Intro:
Warframe is a unique 3rd Person Shooter that combines elements of your average third person shooter with a twist: Character abilities and a "mod" mechanic, allowing you to essentially play whatever Warframe you want, however you want. Deep combat and customization (not physical customization).
THE GOOD:
- The unique "mod" mechanic makes for very deep and thought provoking gameplay and combat, and with the right mindset you can build Warframes to utilise certain abilities, weapons, or gameplay styles.
- Fun combat! Who cares about depth when it isn't fun?
- A Warframe for just about everyone!
- Good Customer Support
THE BAD:
- Only 2-3 weapons per category are viable for use in the end-game, as well as certain Warframe's abilities being rendered useless at the infinitely scaling enemy health bar.
- Good weapons tend to get put in then quickly destroyed via nerfs, and in wanting to allow weapon diversity, it reduces viable weapons to the 2-3 mentioned.
- Most Weapons and Warframes are hidden behind several layers of RNG, causing some Warframes to be nigh unattainable unless you trade for them via real world money's worth of an in-game currency
Overall: This game has many issues. MANY, many issues. It's fun at the end of the day, but albeit, very frustrating at times. I'd say give it a play.

THE BAD:
Warframe's end-game roster is very limited, and despite efforts to make other weapons worth using to increase diversity, most of what they do is nerf. Not just any nerf, but destroy. Weapons, anyway. Warframe balancing is awesome (although how Mesa has not been nerfed yet is beyond me). In trying to increase the roster, they have managed to wittle down what's worth using in total to about
. All of which are locked down behind many walls of RNG. Every time a weapon worthy of use in the Meta is released, it is quickly shoved back into the "NO META FOR YOU" box, effectively removing perfectly good weapons, weapons you spend real money on and lots of time on, might I add, and making them utterly useless. Beware, fellow Tenno.
And don't even get me started on stealth. It's nonexistant. Empty. A shell of something amazing. Cake without yeast. It's that kind of mess. Same goes for Archwing. And Sharkwing. Same deal.
The majority of the elements feel half-a**ed, and thrown in for the sake of a reminder to finish them later, else they'd quickly forget the idea in the first place. Not that that's not what's happening right now, that is.
Mods: You've heard the good. Here's the bad. Some mods are nearly impossible to get, and harder to rank. It takes an incredible amount of work to do. Not only that, but they constantly "fix" locations that will allow us to gear ourselves at some point in this lifetime by being the most efficient with Fusion Cores, XP, and resources (slight hyperbole;
). Not to mention those hard-to-get mods are the best ones. The ones absolutely necessary for the end-game. You will not be successful without them. Period.
They never nerf weapons well, as nerfs always destroy weapons, and buffs are needed for many things but are rarely ever seen. Again, buffs are seen on Warframes just as much as nerfs. Warframes are balanced, weapons are not.
My biggest issue with this game is their tendency to take perfectly viable weapons and mods (ones not on the 11 roster of viable weapons), and beat them to a pulp and throw them away, spitting in the face of anyone who put work into it. You can always make more money... but you can never get more time... days and days of work, all for naught at the press of a few keys by the devs. Be careful in what you craft. Wait a LONG time before you craft it. Make sure it won't get nerfed, and you won't get burned. Like I have many times.
This game is worth playing, but it has many core issues that need to be fixed to keep people coming back. It's no coincidence more veteran players are leaving with each day, and they're losing players just as much as gaining new ones. It's this mentality of f*cking over experienced players and rewarding noobs, and nerfing to oblivion that will ultimately ruin this game if it isn't addressed. Play it while it's here.

Ok. I have enough hours on record to give a review.  I feel like I have come to understand the issues that surround this game.  The problem comes from a simple fact of what this game set out to be is not what it eventually evolved into.  To summarize, Ark: Survival Evolved is pitched as a survival game but in actuality, it is an RTS.
An RTS where a single unit requires hours of investment and bigger units sometimes require days.  But to further elaborate, unless you have joined a server that has only just come up, it is an RTS where you join in after the opponents have already lost and a single army has won the map.  The server isn't big enough for everyone.
But the size of the maps are huge, how is it not big enough for everyone?  The answer is flyers.  Mid game, the thrill of survival is lost as soon as your first flyer is secured.  Early game, you wouldn't think of lugging your convoy too far due to a need for food, shelter, and the dangers of an ever imposing wilderness.  After a flyer is secured, you have to go out of your way to be in any real danger.  The thrill of flying over the landscape is exciting and fun but it actually detracts from the excitement of being in any real danger on the maps themselves.  But this is an addition that is too late to address now that it has been done.
With all of that being said, the game itself is addictive.  Fighting for your right to exist on the map is full of military and political conflict.  The dinos and environment are visually astounding with the right hardware.  The development team, even though they are bad about false promises, actually never fail to deliver regular updates of some kind and are truly as passionate about the game as are the players.
The only caveat is that, being in early access, The game is BADLY unbalanced and in favor of established tribes, but I believe the developers are on the right track to bring the best dino based survival experience to all of us, even if many people will get their toys taken away before we get there.

Do you like Fast Paced Action? How About Parkour Combat? How about Co-op? Like all of those? Good, then this game is for you! Special features include:
- Wasting your cash!
- Grinding Endlessly!
- More Grinding!
- Grinding!
- Crafting Weapons!
- Grinding.
- Multiplayer!
- Grinding.
NOTE: I have played mostly on the PS4 Version recently, so the Stats on my steam account are un-important.

As you can see, I've sunk almost 2,000 hours into this game, and I purchased it for a total of £30 (Base game + DLC). For £30, that is well worth it. It has hundreds of hours of playtime, with lots and lots to do before it gets boring. However, the new price of £50 for the base game alone makes me want to give this game a thumbs down. As you already know, it's poorly optimized and I play with an absolute maximum of 35 fps.
The reason i reccommend this game is the sheer amount of playtime and enjoyment I have got from this game. It's very enjoyable when you are just starting off, for the first 2-3 months i would say. I've been playing on a server (3x PVE) now for 4 months, and racked up 1300 hours on that server alone, and i didnt get bored until 1-2 months ago. Once you have established a substantial base and a number of dinos, the only things to do are breed and build (At least for PVE, I can imaine PVP being more fun here). So for the past 2 months, I have been breeding & taming Rexes, Mosas, Quetzals, Argentavis and Allosaurus whenever possible. As one can imagine, this becomes extremely monotanous and boring especially when all the babies that are hatched arent the levels i need. Thus I have to wait until their 15ish-hour breeding timer is up to try again.
And finally, building. Oh building. In vanilla ARK, building is nt enjoyable. At least for me. So, you go out and spend hours gathering resources to build, and you have the building you want all planned out, and then spend HOURS playing with snap points trying to get the game to place the piece where you want it to and destroying misplaced pieces which wastes even more resources. How fun!
Also, one of the main reasons I kept playing was to play with the new dinos that came out on an *almost* monthly basis, however with the launch of the game at the end of August this is obviously stopping, removing the factor that keeps a lot of players coming back for more.
At the end of the day, you can squeeze out a couple of thousand hours from the game, if you're willing to deal with poor optimization and repetetiveness. Of course, the game is a fantastic idea, so if you really are desparate to tame and ride dinos, go for it, but be prepared to deal with what is stated above.
It is a good game, and I will probably be returning to it in a couple of months, and hopefully squeezing out another 500-1000 hours in a new ARK before i get bored or too angry at the sub-par framerate. I really hope the devs can optimise the game properly, as that will surely attract more people to the game.

Also, one of the main reasons I kept playing was to play with the new dinos that came out on an *almost* monthly basis, however with the launch of the game at the end of August this is obviously stopping, removing the factor that keeps a lot of players coming back for more.
At the end of the day, you can squeeze out a couple of thousand hours from the game, if you're willing to deal with poor optimization and repetetiveness. Of course, the game is a fantastic idea, so if you really are desparate to tame and ride dinos, go for it, but be prepared to deal with what is stated above.
It is a good game, and I will probably be returning to it in a couple of months, and hopefully squeezing out another 500-1000 hours in a new ARK before i get bored or too angry at the sub-par framerate. I really hope the devs can optimise the game properly, as that will surely attract more people to the game.
